extracted.intended_audience: authors, manuscript editors, proofreaders, and publishers (book and journal contributors)
extracted.subtask_short: manuscript preparation for books and journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for preparing, submitting, editing, and proofreading manuscripts (print and electronic) for books and journals, including formatting, front/back matter, navigation and linking in electronic formats, and production-stage responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Navigation in electronic formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Navigation is the basis of any electronic publication, starting with search; EPUB and e-book formats include linked tables of contents and internal links; web-based reference works and apps must allow readers to consult smaller pieces and shuttle through many parts in no particular order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context-sensitive keyword indexing for full-text search; include cross-references and hyperlinked items appropriate to the medium; consider links to popular content or cited-by statistics to show where other readers land; navigation is generally determined by content and structure, so use consistent markup and file formats (see 16.7, 2.34, 1.121).

rubrics_metrics.name: Links in electronic formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Links may be directed to internal content, definitions, author pages, or outside resources; there is no cost to following a hyperlink provided users can step back and forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid too many links, irrelevant links, or broken links which irritate readers; prefer internal cross-references or persistent external identifiers such as DOIs for publisher-created links because they must be maintained and updated; for web works some links can be checked or generated programmatically (e.g., related titles via metadata matching).

rubrics_metrics.name: Front and back matter for electronic formats
rubrics_metrics.description: PDF and most e-book formats retain traditional front matter, but web-based publications may demote ancillary elements (prefaces, copyright information, author info) from front position and make them accessible from margins or menus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include copyright information with each subdocument; provide help and related documentation from any part of a publication; adapt the taxonomy of front/back matter to web contexts (home pages, about links, site maps, help menus); the table of contents may drive top-level navigation in online journals or manuals (see 1.125, 1.118).

rubrics_metrics.name: Orienting the reader in electronic formats
rubrics_metrics.description: E-books often lack fixed page numbers; devices orient readers by location or screen numbers, percentage progress bars, or simple running heads; web publications can display location in hierarchy or provide return-to-top navigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider using location markers, screen numbers, running heads, section or paragraph numbering, or hierarchical navigation based on a table of contents to aid citation and navigation; EPUB may support page number markers to map to print page numbers when using the same workflow (see 2.76, 14.160, 16.2, 16.13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source citations in electronic formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic environment allows linking in-text references to the items they refer to and linking out to cited resources themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply links in any electronic format (PDF, e-book, HTML) but be aware that linked-to items in notes or bibliographies may be presented apart from list context, making traditional bibliographic strategies (e.g., ibid., 3-em dash) impractical (see 14.34, 14.67).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexes in electronic formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Back-of-the-book indexes can be hyperlinked to the text; e-book linking to printed page numbers can be facilitated by adding page-number markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optionally link directly from index terms to locations in the text (more elegant but time-consuming); link to numbered paragraphs when available; use EPUB/structured markup to support page markers (see 16.2, 16.13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript submission checklist (elements to provide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before manuscript editing begins, an author should provide all elements to be included in the work (modeled on parts of a book).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items include: title page; dedication; epigraph; table of contents; list of illustrations; list of tables; preface; acknowledgments; any other front matter; all text matter (introductions, part titles); notes; appendixes; glossary; bibliography/reference list; any other back matter; all illustrations and tables; illustration captions; list of special characters used; abstract(s) and keywords; all permissions in writing for reproduced material; ensure elements are final and up to date including URLs (see 1.76, chapter 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting the manuscript (electronic files and backup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers usually require the latest electronic file(s); authors should make a secure backup and avoid further changes after submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some publishers also require hard copy or PDF as a safeguard—ensure any last-minute changes to electronic files are reflected in hard copy/PDF; include a cover letter with author name, title, total word count, electronic file names, and software used; describe any material not included electronically (artwork) or non-printable items (videos, animations, large data files) specifying software, number, types, and file names; consult publisher-specific instructions (see 2.4, 2.5, 2.7-25, 16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Making changes after submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a final manuscript is submitted the publisher maintains the version of record; authors needing further changes must alert the publisher immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor changes can usually be indicated on the edited document sent back for author review; major changes may require sending a revised manuscript before editing begins and may not be accepted if the publisher has begun work; journals rarely permit major changes after acceptance; peer-reviewed articles requiring major changes may need additional review (see 2.6, 2.71, 2.88).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting a paper-only manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: If submitting typewritten/paper manuscript, authors typically must submit two paper copies and keep a third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All copy must be double-spaced and legible; handwritten additions must be clear and written above the line or in the margin; avoid writing on backs of pages; corrections longer than a short phrase should be a separate document inserted and clearly labeled; use good-quality, standard-size paper (8.5x11 or A4) (see 2.6, 2.43).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers' manuscript-preparation guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Many publishers have specific requirements for software, typeface, and formats for illustrations and tables; these should be followed precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency and simplicity are essential; content (words and order) is more important than presentation; keep structure of chapters and sections clear; a simple presentation is preferable to elaborate formatting; consult typical manuscript editor cleanup routine for what publishers look for (see 2.80).

rubrics_metrics.name: Line spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers customarily require any printout to be double-spaced, including extracts, footnotes/endnotes, bibliographies, and other material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-spacing facilitates pencil editing; consult publisher about any option to send PDF instead of paper; avoid extra space or blank lines between paragraphs; indicate intentional breaks with three asterisks on a line by themselves; stanza breaks in poetry have special guidance (see 2.8, 2.20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Space between sentences and after colons
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a single character space, not two spaces, between sentences and after colons used within a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-structured electronic document should never include more than one consecutive character space; see related sections (2.12, 6.119-21).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification and margins
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscript text should be presented flush left (ragged right), not justified to the right margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use margins of at least one inch on all four sides of hard copy to leave room for handwritten queries; flush-left avoids inconsistent spacing between words and sentences (see 2.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabs versus indents (and types of indents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate tab characters from paragraph indents; use indentation features rather than tabs for most formatting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three basic types of indent: first-line indent (apply to new paragraphs), left indent (apply to all lines of a paragraph), hanging indent (every line but first indented, used for bibliographies/indexes); choose a consistent method and avoid using tabs to achieve indents (except permitted uses such as tab at beginning of paragraph or after number in a vertical list); typical default tab/indent is about half an inch; avoid two or more consecutive tabs and never use tabs within a paragraph except where allowed (see 2.11-2.13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph format
rubrics_metrics.description: Each new paragraph should begin with a first-line indent applied with the Tab key or the word processor's indentation feature; do not use the Space bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use Enter or Tab in the middle of a paragraph; eliminate extra character space or tab after final punctuation; when a paragraph is interrupted by an extract/list/equation the text after the interruption begins flush left unless it's a new paragraph; follow special rules for prose/poetry extracts and lists (see 2.11-2.12, 2.19-2.21).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn off the hyphenation function on the word processor; only use hyphens that would appear regardless of line breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not manually break long words with hyphens (e.g., long URLs); allow ragged right margin rather than inserting manual hyphens; see also 2.96.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an em dash for sentence breaks either with the em dash character or two hyphens (no spaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 3-em dash for repeated bibliography author names is best left to the manuscript editor; insert three em dashes or six unspaced hyphens if necessary; leave en dash usage to editorial responsibility and avoid substituting incorrectly (see 6.78-84, 6.85-94).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics, underline, and boldface
rubrics_metrics.description: Italics should be used where intended; underlining will generally be construed as indicating italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you intend underlining rather than italics to appear, state this clearly to the publisher; use boldface only for words that must appear bold in the published version; in electronically redlined manuscripts underlining may denote editorial changes (see 2.84, fig. 2.4, 2.18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the actual special character your software allows rather than keyboard substitutes; include a list of special characters used in the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When characters are unavailable, enclose a descriptive shorthand in angle brackets (e.g., <bhook>); copy the correct character from Unicode code charts if needed; if planning to use a special font that may not support Unicode, consult the publisher first; provide how each character should look and include Unicode code points if helpful (see tables 11.1-11.2, 11.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format for chapter titles and titles of other parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles for chapters and other parts usually begin on a new page and use upper- and lowercase letters rather than full capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles should match the entries in the table of contents; 'Chapter 1', 'Chapter 2', etc. should appear above numbered-chapter titles (see chapter 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format for subheads
rubrics_metrics.description: Set each subhead on a new line, flush left, and clearly distinguish levels so they can be carried over for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish levels by font size or style; use the word processor's style palette to manage levels; Chicago prefers headline-style capitalization for subheads with no terminal period; run-in heads are italicized and sentence-style with a period (see 8.158-159, 1.56).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format for prose extracts (block quotations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose extracts should be indented from the left margin using the word processor's indentation feature; the first line should not have an additional paragraph indent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If extract contains multiple paragraphs, each new paragraph begins with a first-line indent; use a hard return only at the end of the extract and after any paragraphs within it; extracts have same line spacing as surrounding text and need not be in smaller font; text that follows an extract is indented only if it is a new paragraph, otherwise it begins flush left (see 2.11, 2.19, 13.22-24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format for poetry extracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry extracts should be indented (not centered) and use left indent plus hanging indent for each line; hard returns mark ends of lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let runover lines wrap normally; use a hard return at the end of each full line of poetry but never in the middle of a line; do not use the Tab key for indents; indicate stanza breaks with an extra hard return; if unusual spacing is required append a photocopy or scan of the original; source, if given after the extract, should appear in parentheses on a separate indented line (see 2.20, 13.25-29).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format for lists and outlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Unnumbered lists should use the word processor's indentation feature to assign left and hanging indents; numbered/lettered lists should follow conventions for punctuation and tabs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let runover lines wrap normally and avoid using the Tab key to indent runovers; in numbered or lettered lists, follow each number/letter with a period (or other punctuation) and a tab; bullets followed by a tab; consider using built-in list features but note editors may convert automatically generated numbers/letters to regular text for compatibility; text after a list is indented only if it is a new paragraph (see 2.21, 6.127-32).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format for footnotes and endnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Create notes using the footnote or endnote function to take advantage of automatic renumbering; notes should have same line spacing as manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insert extra hard returns between notes; notes may appear as footnotes or chapter/book endnotes unless publisher requests otherwise; do not mix footnotes and endnotes without necessity; avoid appending note references to chapter titles; number notes to tables separately; follow note form guidance in chapter 14 (see 2.24, 14.24-60).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format for glossaries and lists of abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Each entry should begin on a new line; separate term from definition with a period, colon, or em dash (choose one and use consistently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In glossaries begin the definition with a capital letter and end entries with a period unless entries are incomplete sentences; abbreviations expanded should be capitalized as they would appear in text; consistently italicized terms in text should be italicized in glossary too; entries should have same line spacing and may be flush-and-hang or first-line indented; avoid multiple columns (see 2.25, 1.44, 1.61).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format for bibliographies and reference lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Each bibliography or reference-list entry should begin on a new line and use a hanging indent applied with the word processor's indentation feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never use the Tab key to indent runover lines; use the same line spacing as the rest of the manuscript; follow chapter 14 for capitalization and italics and consider citation-management-software issues (see 2.24, 14.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format for abstracts and keywords
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may be required to submit abstracts and keywords for the book and for individual chapters; book abstracts are single paragraphs up to about 500 words, chapter abstracts shorter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstracts should clearly summarize the book's main arguments and conclusions (or chapter overview); keywords (typically 5–10) accompany the abstract and are designed to enhance visibility in search engines—use significant terms from the abstract and optionally synonyms; each keyword should be a single word or an accepted short compound; abstracts/keywords often form the basis of promotional metadata (see 1.76, 1.93).
